newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel's neighbours losing patience - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Israel's neighbours losing patience - diplomats.

text.p: Israel's Arab neighbours, losing patience after three months of inaction by the new Israeli government, are considering a more robust approach towards peace negotiations, diplomats say.

Arab foreign ministers met in Cairo for more than four hours on Saturday and Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said later they had devised a course of action to put to President Hosni Mubarak, host of a landmark Arab summit in June.
"We discussed many proposals from several Arab countries and we agreed on a specific course, which is in the report I will take to President Mubarak tomorrow," he said.
Moussa declined to give any details but the diplomats said the proposals included a boycott of multilateral talks with Israel and other restrictions on negotiations.
"The proposals are on cutting the negotiations down to size and adopting the same method in the negotiations as Israel is doing now," one diplomatic source said.

Syria and its ally Lebanon have been boycotting the multilateral talks on regional cooperation for years but countries like Egypt and Jordan have argued in the past that such talks help to convince Israel of their good intentions.
Moussa said Mubarak would no doubt want to discuss the report with other Arab heads of state.
Asked if the foreign ministers had discussed the prospects for a Middle economic conference set for Cairo in November, he said: "We discussed all issues related to the Middle East peace process."
Egypt has said there must be tangible progress towards Middle East peace if it is to go ahead with organising the conference, which is meant to integrate Israel into the regional economy.
The meeting on Saturday evening was the second in two days by the 21 Arab states which attended the Cairo summit -- all Arab League members except Iraq.

At a formal Arab League meeting earlier in the day, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat complained that Israel was making only a show of peace and was not serious about implementing agreements it had made with him.

"There is an impasse not only on the Palestinian track but the Syrian and Lebanese tracks, where nothing has been implemented on the agreements signed and agreed upon," Arafat told reporters at the end of the meeting.

"There is an attempt only to make a political show, to give the impression that there is a tendency from the Israelis to move in the right direction, while on the ground there is nothing concrete in our hands," he added.

But after talks with Mubarak in the Mediterranean city of Alexandria, Arafat said he expected to meet Israeli Defence Minister Titzhak Mordechai soon for talks on an Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.

In the first formal resolution from the Arab League meeting, the foreign ministers condemned Turkish, Iranian or any other intervention in northern Iraq and said a proposed Turkish buffer zone there would be a violation of Iraqi territory.

An Arab League statement said the ministers described the situation in northern Iraq as serious as a result of "Turkish violations on the pretext of setting up a so-called security belt or danger zone".

"The Council (of ministers) expressed its extreme concern at developments in the situation as a result of regional interventions which threaten the unity, security and safety of the territory of the Iraqi Republic," said the statement.
"The Council strongly condemns the intervention by some neighbouring countries in the internal affairs of the territory of an Arab League member state."
The statement mentioned Turkey by name but not Iran, which has supported the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan against the Baghdad-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).
The ministers will meet again on Sunday to finish off work on more mundane Arab League business.
